title: Asaf Jahi Dynasty — Rule and Administration

concepts.partName: Asaf Jahi Dynasty — Establishment and Administration (1724–1857)
concepts.bodyMd:
Between 1687 and 1724, after the decline of the Qutb Shahis, Hyderabad Suba was a part of Deccan under Mughal rule. It was only after 1724 that the Asaf Jahs came to power in the Hyderabad region and ruled until 1948 — a span of nearly 225 years. 

The Hyderabad State comprised regions of Karnataka and Maratwada besides the Telangana core, and lay on the Deccan plateau between the Godavari and Krishna rivers. Under Asaf Jahi rule, Hyderabad developed all-round and built its own identity in culture, language, art, architecture, and literature, entering a distinctly modern phase. The founder of this dynasty was Nizam-ul-Mulk, and the Hyderabad State that he founded went on to become the largest princely state in India.

concepts.partName: Ancestors of Nizam-ul-Mulk
concepts.bodyMd:
### Alam Shaik and Khwaja Abid

The ancestry of Nizam-ul-Mulk goes back to **Alam Shaik**, a Sufi scholar (Pandit) belonging to the Bukhara kingdom of Samarkhand and a descendant of the first Khalifa, Abu Bakar. Alam Shaik was a well-learned man across Samarkhand and held the title **Alum-ul-Ulema**. His wife descended from the famous Mir Humdum clan of Samarkhand.

**Khwaja Abid**, son of this couple, left Samarkhand and joined Aurangzeb's service as a Manasabdar.

*   **Rise under Aurangzeb**: In 1680 he helped suppress the revolt of Prince Akbar, Aurangzeb's son, earning the title **'Chin Qilich Khan'** along with jewellery and horses.
*   **Service record**: He assisted in strengthening administration and peace during Aurangzeb's early reign, helped in the conquest of Bijapur (1686), was rewarded as Subedar of Bidar (Jafarabad), and later held charge as Subedar of Ajmer and Multan.
*   **Death**: While marching from Multan to assist in the Golconda campaign, Khwaja Abid lost his right arm in battle and retired to barracks. He died on **30 January 1687** and was buried at Attapur, near Himayatsagar. His severed arm, found on the battlefield three days later and identified by a signet ring, was buried separately at Kismatpura near Golconda; Asaf Jah VII repaired this tomb in 1942.

### Mir Shihabuddin Siddiqui (Firoz Jung)

Khwaja Abid had five sons; the eldest was **Mir Shihabuddin Siddiqui**. Born at Samarkhand in 1649, he reached Delhi in 1668 to meet his father and was appointed mansabdar of 300/70 by Aurangzeb.

**Titles and campaigns**

*   Earned the title **'Khan'** for his role in the Mughal campaign against the Rana of Udaipur.
*   Earned **'Firoz Jung'** for success against an attack by Shambaji.
*   Earned **'Farzund Arjumand'** for valour during the Bijapur campaign.
*   Took part as army chief in the 1687 conquest of Golconda and subjugated the Udgir and Adoni forts.
*   In 1705, defeated the Sindhia of Malwa and was made Subedar of Elichpur, Berar and Gujarat, receiving the title **'Sipah Salar'**.

He married Safiya Khanam, daughter of Saadulla Khan Bahadur (Wazir of Shah Jahan). Late in his career he was blinded by smallpox and died in Gujarat in 1711. Their eldest son was **Mir Qamruddin**, who later took the title Nizam-ul-Mulk and established an independent state in Deccan.

concepts.partName: Nizam-ul-Mulk — Early Career at the Mughal Court
concepts.bodyMd:
Mir Qamruddin (Nizam-ul-Mulk) was born on **11 August 1671** at Agra, son of Ghaziuddin Firoz Jung and Safiya Khanam. As an infant he was named "Nek Bhakt" (fortunate). At age six he visited the Mughal court and drew Aurangzeb's attention; the emperor at once appointed him Mansabdar of 450 horses, doubled a year later.

**Rise through military service**

| Year | Event | Reward/Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1688 | Captured Adoni fort (age 17) with his father | Mansabdar of 2000/500, Arabian horse, jewellery |
| — | Courage in early conquests | Title **'Khan'** |
| 1698 | Occupied Nagori near Bijapur; then captured Nagarkot | Ornated dagger; Mansabdar raised to 3000/500, then 3500/3000, then 4000/3000 |
| 1700 | Cut off supply lines to Parali fort (after fall of Satara) | Helped Mughal occupation of the fort |
| 1705 | Attacked Wajinjar fort in Berar with Aurangzeb, assisted by Tarbiyat Khan | Two Arab horses studded with gold; Mansabdari raised to 5000/5000, plus 1 crore 50 lakh dhams, an elephant, and jewellery |

By this stage Aurangzeb had begun taking Chin Qilich Khan's advice in administrative matters.

**Bijapur retreat and Aurangzeb's death**: With Aurangzeb's permission, Chin Qilich Khan went to Bijapur to arrange a retreat for the ageing emperor at Devapur. Aurangzeb fell sick there and was cared for by Chin Qilich Khan, who was honoured with a ring bearing the title **'Chin Qilich Khan Bahadur'**. In 1706 he was made Fauzdar of Feroznagar Fort. Aurangzeb died on 28 March 1707.

concepts.partName: Nizam-ul-Mulk Through the Mughal Wars of Succession
concepts.bodyMd:
A prolonged struggle for the Mughal throne followed Aurangzeb's death, and Chin Qilich Khan navigated it carefully without taking sides until his position was secure.

1.  **Azam Shah's brief reign**: Azam Shah declared himself emperor amid the succession dispute. Chin Qilich Khan and his son stayed away from the contest. To win him over, Azam raised his Mansabdari to 7000/7000 and gave the title **'Khan-e-Duran'**. Azam Shah died in the war of succession.
2.  **Bahadur Shah I (1707–1712)**: His brother Muazzam succeeded as Bahadur Shah I, reconfirmed Chin Qilich Khan's earlier titles, and posted him as Subedar of Oudh Suba and Faujdar of Lucknow (1707), then in charge of Awadh administration from 9 December 1707. During this period Chin Qilich Khan showed little interest in state affairs, distributed his wealth to the poor, and withdrew from politics for a time.
3.  **Succession crisis of 1712**: On Bahadur Shah I's death at Lahore, his four sons contested the throne.
    *   Chin Qilich Khan marched toward Lahore with 3000 Turani soldiers to support Prince Azam us Shan, but learned en route that Azam us Shan, Jahan Shah, and Rafi us Shan had all been killed, and Jahandar Shah had seized the throne. Disillusioned, he retired for five years into the company of musicians, poets, and intellectuals.
    *   He declined Jahandar Shah's request to re-enter administration despite receiving fresh titles — 'Ghaziuddin Khan', Bahadur Feroz Jung, and Fateh Jung — and a posting to safeguard Agra.
4.  **Farrukhsiyar's accession and the title 'Nizam-ul-Mulk'**: An understanding was reached that Chin Qilich Khan would stay neutral between Jahandar Shah and Farrukh Siyar.
    
    *   Though it was believed his neutrality in practice favoured Farrukh Siyar, and when Farrukh Siyar became emperor, he rewarded Chin Qilich Khan with the title 'Nizam-ul-Mulk', appointing him Subedar of six Subas of Deccan and Faujdar of Karnataka, along with an ornate Arabian horse, royal turban, jewelled sword, and jewellery.
    *   By age 43, his name and fame in the Mughal empire had reached its peak — a standing he would hold for another 35 years until his death.

concepts.partName: First Tenure as Subedar of Deccan
concepts.bodyMd:
Nizam-ul-Mulk reached Aurangabad by June 1713 to take up the Deccan subedari amid volatile and economically poor conditions.

**Checking Maratha revenue claims**: Since 1707 the Marathas had been collecting chauth and sardeshmukhi in Aurangabad Suba from the then Mughal prince Azam Shah, enforcing their domination. Disliking this, Nizam-ul-Mulk discontinued tax collection around Aurangabad first, instructing his Faujdars and Zilladars to drive away Raja Sahu's tax-collecting Tahsildars.

**Revenue reforms**: He introduced a uniform revenue policy in Aurangabad Suba, deputed Shaik Muhammad Azad and Diwan Khembiran (Diwan-i-Sarkar) to correct the corruption of Dawood Khan (a Maratha agent) at Sagar and Amardh, focused on efficient revenue administration across the Deccan subas without overburdening peasants, punished corrupt officials, and kept a close watch on prices — measures that raised both income and productivity.

### Nizam-ul-Mulk's Relations with the Marathas (Early Phase)

Nizam-ul-Mulk was as much a political strategist as a soldier, and he exploited the rivalry between the Maratha rulers of Kolhapur and Satara.

*   Raja Sahu of Kolhapur sent his envoy Haibat Rao, and Chandrasen Jadav of Satara sent his governor Appa Rao, to open dialogue with Nizam-ul-Mulk.
*   After a meeting at Aurangabad involving Rambajirao Nimalkar and Sarjarao Ghatne, both Sarjarao Ghatne and Chandrasen Jadhav defected from the Marathas to Nizam-ul-Mulk's camp.
*   In return, Chandrasen Jadhav received a Mansabdari of 7000/7000 and jagirs at Balki, Brahmanabad, Illandur, and Chandarghad (worth 25 lakh revenue); a fort was built at Chandargadh against the Marathas. Sarjarao received a jagir at Kagal.
*   After consolidating his position, Nizam-ul-Mulk massed his army on the Godavari to display his strength. Raja Sahu and his Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath made counter-preparations, and the two sides fought at Purandhar, where Nizam-ul-Mulk emerged victorious. A treaty followed between Nizam and Balaji Vishwanath, under which Poona and the forts lost by Sahu were handed to Chandrasen Jadav in return for his service.

concepts.partName: Retaining the Subedari of Deccan & Nizam-ul-Mulk as Wazir
concepts.bodyMd:
### Retaining the Subedari of Deccan

Both Nizam-ul-Mulk and the Sayyed Brothers sought to dethrone the ruling Mughals from Delhi. Simultaneously, Nizam-ul-Mulk sought to retain the Deccan subedari for himself.

*   On **9 May 1719**, vexed with the Sayyed brothers' court politics, Nizam-ul-Mulk moved toward Deccan, accompanied by the Faujdar of Bijapur Rustum Khan Beg; at Burhanpur, Rambaji Nimbalkar and Prince Sahu (son of Maratha ruler Rajaram) joined him. Here he exposed the Sayyed brothers' plot and led a movement against their domination of the Mughal court.
*   Fearing him, the Sayyed brothers sent two military expeditions against Nizam-ul-Mulk in **1720** — one under Dilawar Khan, the other under Alam Ali Khan. Nizam-ul-Mulk defeated both, and the emperor, left without option, issued a farman confirming him as Subedar of Deccan.

### Nizam-ul-Mulk as Wazir

Muhammad Amir Khan (prime minister) died in February 1721 and Inayatulla Khan succeeded him. Nizam-ul-Mulk was invited to the Mughal Durbar at Delhi; he appointed Ijjat ud Daula as his representative in Deccan and set out in January 1722, escorted with honour by Shamsud Daula. He was appointed **Wazir (prime minister)** of the Mughal Empire and honoured with a diamond ring, a jewel-studded dagger, and royal cloaks.

**Difficulties as Wazir**

*   Court intrigue and treachery against him increased, and even the emperor began to believe the complaints made against him.
*   He tried to end the Sayyed brothers' court politics and to abolish the Peshkash and Ijara systems, which he viewed as degrading the emperor's prestige by functioning as bribery rather than taxation.
*   He pushed to revive court traditions from the times of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, including reintroduction of the **Jijya tax** on non-believers, and supported the Persians against the Afghans to check Afghan influence in Mughal politics.
*   Court officials feared that success for these policies would make Nizam-ul-Mulk's name and fame grow unchecked; the emperor, though unable to reject him outright, avoided implementing his suggestions.

Dejected, Nizam-ul-Mulk resigned the Wazir post and left Delhi for Muradabad. By the time he reached Agra, the Marathas had attacked Malwa and Gujarat (then under his elder son Ghaziuddin's control), so he sought and obtained permission to mobilize against them. 

By the time he reached the Narmada, the Marathas had already retreated; he then rested at Sirha near Sironj, where he learned of a plot by Mubariz Khan in the Deccan, and by 1724 marched to Aurangabad. Mediation efforts by Khalifa Diwan and Raja Gujarimal Saksena to clear Nizam-ul-Mulk's name with Emperor Muhammad Shah stopped after Raja Gujarimal's death in December 1723.

concepts.partName: The Battle of Shakarkheda and Founding of Asaf Jahi Rule (1724)
concepts.bodyMd:
With no option but to move to Deccan as its Subedar, Nizam-ul-Mulk again sought to reclaim the charge he had assigned to Ijjat ud Daula as his Naib.

*   In February 1724, his enemies at court arranged for **Abdul Mabat Khan**, son of Mubariz Khan, to be appointed Deccan Subedar on behalf of the minor Prince Shahriyar. After the young prince's death, Mubariz Khan declared himself Deccan Subedar, appropriated five lakhs from the treasury, and raised an army from revenue funds.
*   From his base at Siroha, Nizam-ul-Mulk tracked these developments and, on being informed of Mubariz Khan's movement from Hyderabad, marched for Aurangabad via Malwa to neutralize him.
*   Emperor Muhammad Shah ultimately declared Mubariz Khan Subedar of Deccan and transferred Nizam-ul-Mulk's wazirship and subedari charges elsewhere, though he was given the option of staying on in the Deccan Suba.
*   Defying the emperor, Mubariz Khan marched on Aurangabad. Nizam-ul-Mulk wrote repeatedly asking him not to shed innocent blood, but all efforts failed, and the two armies met at **Shakarkheda in Berar** for a final showdown on **23 October 1724**.
*   Nizam-ul-Mulk won the battle; Mubariz Khan died in it. Soldiers and common people welcomed Nizam-ul-Mulk, who thereby became Subedar of the six Deccan subas — **Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar, Bijapur, Khandesh, and Hyderabad**. The Mughal emperor accepted this and conferred on him the title **'Asaf Jah'**.

This victory marked the start of Nizam rule in Deccan (1724 AD), and the dynasty he founded — the Asaf Jahi dynasty — lasted nearly 225 years, ending only with Mir Osman Ali Khan's rule in 1948.

concepts.partName: Nizam-ul-Mulk's Position and Administration as Subedar of Deccan
concepts.bodyMd:
**Political standing**: Politically his position was formally no more than a Sipah Salar or Subedar, though titles such as Nizam-ul-Mulk Fatehjung, Sipah Salar, and Asaf Jah appeared in Mughal farmans. He was appointed Wazir/Vakil-e-Mutluk of the Mughal Empire — once appointed, a Wazir was traditionally never removed. Vakil-e-Mutluk ranked higher in designation than Wazir. Though rarely present at the capital, he was exempted from attendance owing to his experience, recognition, and loyalty.

**Loyalty to the Mughal throne**: Nizam-ul-Mulk never intended to sever Hyderabad from the Mughal Empire. He had the Qutba read in the name of Emperor Muhammad Shah at Friday prayers, minted coins in the emperor's name in Deccan, and all letters and decrees he issued bore the emperor's signature. His subedari was raised to **9000/9000 (duaspa)** on becoming Subedar of Deccan. He regarded himself, throughout, as a servant of the Mughal Empire.

**Administrative charge**: As Subedar of Deccan he took on civil, legal, legislative, and military responsibilities, ran an independent administration with the help of Diwans, organized his own army, raised his own flag, and appointed his own officers — while still maintaining cordial relations with the Mughal Empire.

### Revenue System — Serf-i-Khas and Diwani

He used wealth generated in the Suba — from mines, mineral wealth, diamond mines, and war booty — and divided his Deccan Suba into three parts:

*   **1/3rd** kept directly under his own control, known as **Serf-i-Khas**, to meet state expenditure.
*   **2/3rds**, known as **Diwani**, distributed among officers and persons he deemed loyal.
*   Jagirdars, Zamindars, and Deshmukhs, in return for recognition of their positions, gave him gifts called **Nazaranas**.

### Territorial Expansion

Under Nizam-ul-Mulk's state, expansion took place between the **Narmada in the north and the Kaveri river in the south**, and between **Bijapur in the west and Machilipatnam in the east**. Coming from Malwa, he brought along many Muslim and Hindu followers who had backed his success in Deccan; he appointed Muslims to military posts and Hindus to administrative posts, rewarding both with jagirs.

### Conflict with the Marathas (1725–1728)

Nizam-ul-Mulk took steps to abolish the collection of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi by the Marathas in his state. This led to war with the Marathas beginning **August 1727**, continuing till **March 1728**. Nizam-ul-Mulk was defeated at **Palkhed**, near Daultabad, and was forced to sign a treaty: Chatrapati Sahu was recognized as ruler of the Marathas, and Nizam-ul-Mulk agreed to permit the Marathas to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi in the Deccan.

concepts.partName: Invasion of Nadir Shah and the Mediation of Nizam-ul-Mulk (1738)
concepts.bodyMd:
Nadir Shah invaded India in 1738 after crossing the Hindukush. Nizam-ul-Mulk sent his army to Karnal to join the Mughal contingent, but it failed to check the invader. Nadir Shah looted Delhi, and Emperor Muhammad Shah, unable to stop the devastation, asked Nizam-ul-Mulk to negotiate with him.

*   As Mughal ambassador, Nizam-ul-Mulk not only extended talks but influenced Nadir Shah through direct appeal, warning him that killing could not continue once none were left alive to kill. Nadir Shah stopped the killings and offered Nizam-ul-Mulk the Mughal throne, which he refused.
*   Emperor Muhammad Shah, satisfied with how he had handled the crisis, awarded him further titles: 'Amir ul Umra Bakshi ul Mumlik', Jamlat ul Mulk, Madrul Maham, Nizam-ul-Mulk, Bahadur Fathejung, Mominus Sultanat, Shuruknus Sultanat, Asaf Jah.

concepts.partName: Character, Achievements, and Death of Nizam-ul-Mulk
concepts.bodyMd:
**Career profile**: Nizam-ul-Mulk served under eight Mughal emperors between Aurangzeb and Muhammad Shah, actively serving four of them. He chose Deccan, not Delhi, as his centre of power, having governed there three separate times — **1713–1715, 1720–1722, and 1724 till his death** — administering Deccan continuously for thirty years in his final tenure. He took part in 87 battles over his lifetime.

**Character**: Though he occupied the highest positions in Mughal administration, he lived simply and was regarded by others, and occasionally even by emperors, as a protector figure. He was a man of character and values who avoided treachery, treason, and deceit — earning him widespread respect. He is regarded as the most extraordinary ruler of eighteenth-century India; his efficiency was such that even Nadir Shah offered him the Mughal throne.

**Cultural side**: He was proficient in Persian and Turkish, composed Persian poetry under the pen name **'Shakir'**, and shared his experiences during his leisure time. His personal assistant, Lala Mansaram, compiled ninety such stories reflecting his mental maturity, intelligence, analytical knowledge, and love of nature.

**Death and succession**: Nizam-ul-Mulk died in **1748** at the age of 76 and was buried at Shaik Burhanuddin Garib Chisti Mazar, Khulabad, near Aurangabad — the same site as Aurangzeb's tomb.

*   He was survived by five sons and a daughter: Mir Ghaziuddin Siddique Bahadur Firoj Jung, Mir Ahmad Ali Khan Siddique Bahadur Nasar Jung, Sayyad Mahamud Khan Siddique Bahadur Salabat Jung, Mir Nizam Ali Khan Siddique Bahadur Fatehjung, and Mir Mahamud Sharif Khan Siddique Bahadur Basalat Jung. 
*   At his death, his elder son Ghaziuddin was serving at the Mughal court. A war of succession broke out among his sons, which the English and French East India Companies successfully exploited to dominate the Deccan and its trade and commerce.

* * *

concepts.partName: The Carnatic Civil War
concepts.bodyMd:
The Hyderabad State was the largest state in India. After Nizam-ul-Mulk's death, civil war broke out over succession, and this coincided with growing European intervention in state politics — a period this section covers between **1748 and 1857**, tracing the civil war, the state's position, and its relations with Europeans.

Under the rule of the first Nizam, Carnatic was under the control of Deccan Subedar Nizam-ul-Mulk. Sadatullah Khan, the childless Nawab of Carnatic, had adopted his two sons-in-law, Dost Ali and Bakar Ali. Sadatullah got Mughal permission to appoint **Dost Ali** as his political successor without informing the Nizam. Once enthroned, Dost Ali refused to pay taxes to the Subedar.

**Maratha intervention**: Angered, Nizam-ul-Mulk decided to act, but before he could, Maratha rulers under Ragoji Bhonsle and Fatheh Singh invaded Carnatic in 1740 for chauth collection, attacked Arcot, and defeated Chanda Sahib (ruler of Tiruchinapally and Dost Ali's son-in-law), taking him prisoner to Satara. 

*   Dost Ali died at Damerlacheruvu defending Arcot. The Marathas then appointed **Safdar Ali** as Nawab of Carnatic and **Murari Rao Gherpade** as ruler of Tiruchinapally, with Safdar Ali required to pay 40 lakh rupees to the Marathas as chauth compensation; Nizam-ul-Mulk separately ordered him to clear all dues and taxes.
*   Safdar Ali raised taxes across Carnatic to meet these demands, causing widespread public discontent.

**Succession chaos**: Safdar Ali's brother-in-law, Murtiza Ali Khan of Nellore, was unhappy over the tax rises and killed Safdar Ali with the help of Safdar Ali's own wife and sister. Murtiza Ali's attempt to declare himself ruler angered Carnatic's Mokasadars and Amirs. **Syed Muhammad Khan**, Safdar Ali's son, became ruler of Carnatic in 1742.

**Nizam-ul-Mulk's settlement**: Nizam-ul-Mulk came to Carnatic and restored peace, appointing Sayeed Muhammad Khan as Nawab of Arcot and Anwaruddin Khan as his protector, while sending the Marathas back from Tiruchirapally. Conditions improved by 1744, and Nizam-ul-Mulk returned to Deccan. 

*   War then broke out on the east coast between the French and English; when Anwaruddin (Nawab of Carnatic) sent his son Mahfuz Khan to help the British, the French defeated him. Nizam-ul-Mulk sent his son **Nasir Jung** to Carnatic in 1747 to restore peace, appointing him Nawab of Arcot, Kadapa, and Kondanur, with powers to collect dues from Mysore. 
*   In 1748 Nasir Jung came to Aurangabad on news of his father's illness. Nizam-ul-Mulk, founder of the Asaf Jahi dynasty, died in **June 1748**.

concepts.partName: First Carnatic War (1746–1748)
concepts.bodyMd:
The three Carnatic Wars reshaped politics across Southern India.

**Causes**

*   Commercial rivalry between the French and English East India Companies, both seeking a monopoly over trade in Southern India.
*   French Governor **Dupleix**'s aim to drive the English out of India, which made war increasingly likely.
*   The **Austrian Succession War** (1740–1748) in Europe, in which England and France backed opposite sides — England supporting Austria (Queen Maria Theresa, 1740–1780) and France supporting Prussia (Frederick II, 1740–1786) — extended its consequences into Southern India.

**Course of the war**: With no favourable conditions for the French in Carnatic, Dupleix asked Nawab Anwaruddin to prevent a British attack on the French company. Anwaruddin secured English agreement to maintain peace, and when the English commander Bornet captured French ships on a complaint from Dupleix, Anwaruddin ordered their return and had Bornet sent back to England.

In July 1746, the French Mauritius Governor **Labordinies** arrived at Coromandel with ships and army; Dupleix and Labordinies jointly captured **Madras** in September 1746. The British sought Anwaruddin's help; Labordinies initially agreed to return Madras for 1,00,000 Pagodas, but Dupleix refused and recaptured it. 

When Anwaruddin ordered Dupleix to hand Madras to the British, Dupleix refused, and Anwaruddin sent his army against the French — the resulting **Battle of Adayar** (Santhome, 1746) ended in defeat for the Nawab's forces, leaving Madras under full French control.

**Aftermath**: The Austrian Succession War concluded with the **Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)**; Prussia won and occupied Silesia, and per the treaty both companies in India returned to their original centres — France returning Madras to the British, a considerable humiliation for the British given Dupleix's rising fame. 

Both sides released captured soldiers. The war exposed Anwaruddin's weakness, the Nawab's outdated weapons, and the lack of a regular navy — factors that reduced the standing of both the Nizam and the Mughal power in the region.

concepts.partName: Second Carnatic War (1749–1754)
concepts.bodyMd:
This war began as a succession struggle between local rulers.

*   **Anwaruddin vs Chanda Sahib**: Chanda Sahib, grandson of Dost Ali and holder of Mughal-recognized succession rights, had been captured and jailed at Satara during Maratha attacks. After Nizam-ul-Mulk's death, the Marathas released him; on reaching Carnatic he declared himself Nawab. Anwaruddin tried to control him.
*   **Deccan succession dispute**: With Nizam-ul-Mulk's death in 1748, a parallel dispute erupted over the Deccan subedari — his grandson **Muzafar Jung** declared himself the rightful successor. The French, drawn into both disputes, recognized Chanda Sahib as Nawab of Carnatic and Muzafar Jung as Subedar of Deccan, backing both.
*   **Battle of Ambur (1749)**: Chanda Sahib, Muzafar Jung, and Dupleix's combined forces fought Anwaruddin at Ambur (near Vellore) in August 1749. Anwaruddin was defeated and died; his son **Muhammad Ali** escaped to Tiruchirapally. Chanda Sahib, with French help, took the Carnatic throne, and rewarded the French with the region between Coromandel and Pondicherry plus valuable gifts.
*   **British counter-move**: The British, siding with Nasir Jung and Muhammad Ali, saw Nasir Jung reach Carnatic in 1750 and send ambassadors (Meropanth and Qaze Dayem) demanding the surrender of Muzafar Jung, Chanda Sahib, and Dupleix — diplomacy failed. On 18 March 1750, Mughal forces occupied Gingi; Chanda Sahib, beset by Maratha and Muhammad Ali pressure, fled to Pondicherry, and Muzafar Jung surrendered, protected without cruelty by the Nizam's Peshkar Ramdas Pandit.
*   **Death of Nasir Jung and rise of Muzafar Jung**: Pathan Nawabs in Nasir Jung's own camp — Abdul Nabi Khan of Kadapa, Himmat Khan Bahadur of Kurnool, Abdul Karim Khan of Savanoor, and the Nawab of Bankapur — turned on him; Nasir Jung was killed in firing by the Kurnool Nawab, and the Kadapa Nawab beheaded him, carrying the news to Muzafar Jung. 

*   On **31 December 1750**, Muzafar Jung declared himself Sultan in a grand Darbar, distributed 50,000 pounds to French officials, gave Dupleix the title **'Jafar Jung'**, and appointed Nawabs for Carnatic, Mysore, and the region south of the Krishna, handing Masulipatnam, Yanam, and Karaikal to the French.

*   **Death of Muzafar Jung and rise of Salabat Jung**: The Pathan Nawabs conspired against Muzafar Jung; the two sides fought near Rayachoti (25 miles south of Kadapa) in January 1751. Abdul Karim Khan (Nawab of Savanoor) died and the Kurnool Nawab was gravely wounded, but Muzafar Jung was killed. 

*   The French officer **Bussy** immediately declared **Salabat Jung**, another son of Nizam-ul-Mulk, as Nawab of Hyderabad (1751). Salabat Jung gave Kondapalli, Guntur, Elluru, Rajahmundry, and Chikakole (Srikakulam) to the French, and Dupleix was made Governor of the coastal regions south of the Krishna — sharply raising French influence.

*   **British counter-offensive**: Taking Sandars' advice, the British concluded a treaty with Muhammad Ali of Tiruchirapally and, with Robert Clive and Lawrence, attacked Chanda Sahib, who was killed. Muhammad Ali was made Nawab of Arcot. 

*   The British defeated the French at Arcot, Aarani, and Kaveripak, establishing British power in Carnatic. Dupleix lost the confidence of the French government and returned to France; in 1759 the French officer **Gadehue** concluded the **Treaty of Pondicherry** with the British — neither side would interfere in local politics, both would recognize existing Mughal designations, and both returned to their prior centres.
*   Bussy remained in Deccan pursuing French interests there, while the British announced support for Salabat Jung — closing the Second Carnatic War.

concepts.partName: Battle of Bobbili (1757)
concepts.bodyMd:
Zamindars across the region revolted against French power in Deccan — notably Shah Nawab Khan of Rajahmundry and Fouzdar Ibrahim Khan of Chicacole (Srikakulam), while **Vijaya Rama Raju** alone sided with the French. Bussy came from Hyderabad to Rajahmundry on 19 December 1756 (via Bezawada and Elluru) to suppress the Circar revolts. Ibrahim Khan escaped to the ruler of Bobbili. Other Zamindars surrendered, but the **ruler of Bobbili, Raja Ranga Rao**, remained independent and refused to submit.

Vijaya Rama Raju instigated the French to attack Bobbili and to strip its Zamindari rights. Ranga Rao learned of this but refused to leave. When 30 French soldiers passing through Bobbili territory were killed, Bussy declared war on **24 January 1757**.

*   Ranga Rao sent Ibrahim Khan away safely, then defended his fort with Vijaya Rama Raju, Hyder Jung, and the Zamindar of Peddapuram fighting on the French side.
*   Realising defeat was inevitable, Ranga Rao ordered the women in his fort to be killed and set all houses on fire; his forces fought to the end, and he himself died of a bullet wound. The French won and took revenue and other spoils; when French soldiers entered the fort, they were shocked by what they found. Ranga Rao's son was saved by the servant **Dasi Lakshmi**, and Bussy welcomed and protected the boy.
*   **Tandra Papaiah**, Bobbili's representative, learned of the war, gathered his friends Devulapalli Peddanna and Buddha Raju Venkaiah, and after three days killed **Vijaya Rama Raju**.

Bussy received 2,00,000 from Bobbili's Zamindari revenue. Except for the Gumperu tenant (Palegar), all tenants in Bobbili began paying taxes to Bussy; after this war, all Zamindars paid land revenue regularly to the French, and French influence increased across the coastal region.

concepts.partName: Third Carnatic War (1756–1763)
concepts.bodyMd:
The dispute arose again between the French and English in Europe, both sides being on opposite ends of the **Seven Years' War** (started 17 May 1756) between Austria (Queen Maria Theresa) and Prussia (Frederick II) over Silesia — with consequences again playing out in Carnatic (the war there began in 1758). France sent **Count-de-Lali**, who lacked knowledge of Indian conditions — a fact that favoured the British; in 1758 Lali reached Pondicherry and attacked Tanjavur but failed.

**British consolidation**: Robert Clive's victory in the **Battle of Plassey (1757)** established British power in Bengal. After Plassey, British forces joined Carnatic and prepared to attack Madras and Tanjavur. Lali ordered French officer Bussy to leave Hyderabad for Carnatic; the Nizam's Nawab thereupon declared support for the British, since he disliked Bussy's domination at his court. Robert Clive attacked the French-held Northern Circars.

*   The **Chandurti War** (7 December 1758) saw British forces, aided by **Ananda Gajapati** (son-in-law of Vijaya Rama Raju, holding Vijayanagaram Zamindari succession rights and maintaining good relations with the British of Madras), capture Visakhapatnam, Chebrole village, and finally win at Chandurti under Colonel Ford, chasing the French away. British forces under Captain Nocks and Maclein captured Rajahmundry.
*   The British occupied Northern Circars and concluded a treaty with **Salabat Jung on 14 May 1759**, under which Salabat Jung gave up eight districts in the Circars — Masulipatnam, Nizampatnam, Kondaveedu, and Akulamanadu — to the British. This was the **first political treaty between the British and the Nizam**, and marked a turning point for British dominance in Hyderabad State.
*   Count-de-Lali and Bussy jointly tried but failed to attack Madras. British officer **Sir Eyre Coote** defeated the French and captured Bussy as prisoner in the **Wandwasi War (1760)**; Lali surrendered to the British on 16 January 1761.
*   In 1763 the Seven Years' War concluded with the **Treaty of Paris**: Prussia's King Frederick prevailed and the British too gained, since Austria lost Silesia entirely. 

*   The French were defeated in the Third Carnatic War and restricted to Pondicherry; the remaining French centres were destroyed. With the French defeated, there was no opponent left to the British in India, and the Carnatic Nawab became a British puppet after this war — though the British still maintained good relations with the rulers of Hyderabad State for a time.

concepts.partName: Nizam–British Relations Under Nizam Ali Khan
concepts.bodyMd:
During Salabat Jung's rule (1751–1762) as Subedar of Deccan, French dominance grew in Hyderabad following control of the Northern Circars, which the Nizam disliked. Princes **Nizam Ali Khan** and **Basalat Jung** criticized the French and were consequently captured and sent to Daulatabad fort by Salabat Jung. The Marathas then attacked and captured Ahmadnagar fort.

**Rise of Nizam Ali Khan**

*   Salabat Jung, watching Maratha actions, reconciled with his brother Nizam Ali Khan, released him from Daulatabad, and appointed him Subedar of Berar (1757).
*   Nizam Ali fought the Marathas twice — first in December 1757, concluding a treaty with the Peshwa at Sindkhed and giving up Darur fort and Rs. 25,00,000 as levy; and again in 1759 at **Udgir**, where he was defeated and had to cede Ahmadnagar, Daulatabad, Burhanpur, and Bijapur to the Marathas.
*   After the Marathas were themselves defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali in the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**, Peshwa Baji Rao (who never recovered from the Udgir defeat) died in June 1761. Nizam Ali seized the moment, attacked Pune, and destroyed the city. In January 1762, Peshwa Madhava Rao concluded a treaty with Nizam Ali, ceding regions worth Rs. 27,00,000 revenue; Nizam Ali also captured Naldurg during the Pune attacks and destroyed the Sindhia treasury building at Srigonda.
*   Salabat Jung welcomed Nizam Ali back at Bidar after the Pune war and agreed that Salabat Jung would remain Subedar of Deccan while Nizam Ali conducted state administration. On **6 July 1762**, Nizam Ali captured and killed his brother Salabat Jung, declaring himself Nizam of Hyderabad — the first ruler to adopt the title **'Nizam'**, which became the dynasty's hereditary style from then on. In 1762 the British identified Nizam Ali as a useful friend.

**Northern Circars question**: Conditions in the Northern Circars were unfavourable after Ananda Gajapati's death (1760). Salabat Jung had issued a Sanad (Charter of rights) to Colonel Ford and officer James Alexander of Masulipatnam, but they failed to secure Nizam Ali's approval for it. 

Nizam Ali instead appointed Hussain Ali Khan as Fauzdar of Elluru, Rajahmundry, and Mustafanagar, and assigned Chicacole revenue collection to the king of Vijayanagaram — all of which created British tension, since the British had not helped Nizam Ali against the Marathas, and he in turn acted strictly against them.

*   In 1764, the British succeeded in the **Battle of Buxar** against Bengal's Nawab, the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam, and the Nawab of Ayodhya; a treaty at Allahabad (1765) gave Northern Circars to the British company via a Mughal firman. Nizam Ali did not recognize this firman, creating problems for the British.
*   The British sent **Kandregula Jogi Panthulu**, a well-connected Dubasi (agent for tax collection), to negotiate; he had good relations with Diwan Ruknudoula in Hyderabad. Amid revolts in Rajahmundry (which Nizam Ali went to suppress with Ruknuddoula) and among Nizam forces at Gollapudi (over unpaid salaries), Jogi Panthulu used the moment to secure Nizam Ali's agreement to give five Northern Circar districts to the British on contract for Rs. 9,00,000.
*   On **12 November 1766**, the British (represented by General Kailand and General Smith) concluded a treaty: Rajahmundry, Elluru, Mustafanagar, Murtizanagar, and Chicacole Circars were leased to the company for Rs. 9,00,000 per year — four lakhs for Rajahmundry, Elluru, and Mustafanagar combined, two lakhs each for Murtizanagar and Chicacole. 

*   Basalat Jung, Nizam Ali's brother, had received Murtizanagar as jagir in 1761; the company was to take over that Jagir and continue lease payments only after Basalat Jung's death or loss of the Nizam's faith.

*   Though reluctant, the Nizam's poor economic conditions forced him to give up the Northern Circars. He was further angered and, seeking Mysore support, came to an understanding with Hyder Ali to remove Muhammad Ali (seen as a British puppet) and install Tipu Sultan as Nawab of Carnatic. 

*   The British, moving first against Hyder Ali, defeated Nizam Ali's forces at Tiruchirapally. 
*   On **23 February 1768**, Nizam Ali concluded a new treaty with the Madras British Company recognizing Muhammad Ali as real ruler of Carnatic, ceding Diwani (civil administration, revenue) rights on Balaghat of Carnatic to the British for a yearly payment of Rs. 7,00,000 — effectively removing the Nizam's powers over Carnatic and the Northern Circars.

### Possession of Guntur Circar

Prior to the British treaty, Murtizanagar (Guntur) was under Basalat Jung. The Elluru, Rajahmundry, Mustafanagar, and Chicacole Circars had already passed to the British in 1766. In the case of Murtizanagar, it was only to pass to the company after Basalat Jung's death or loss of Nizam Ali's confidence.

Basalat Jung, in conflict with his brother, recruited French troops and held talks with the British against Nizam Ali. Pressured by the British, he concluded a treaty on **27 January 1779**, removing the French from his employment and handing Guntur Circar to the British — angering Nizam Ali, who protested in writing. 

British officer Holland relayed the Nizam's anger to the Bengal Government; Governor-General **Warren Hastings**, recognizing the resentment, assured the Nizam of continued friendship, and the British returned Guntur to Basalat Jung. Basalat Jung died in 1782; after discussion with **Cornwallis**, Nizam Ali handed Guntur over to the British permanently on **18 September 1788** — placing the entire coastal Andhra region from Ganjam to Guntur under British control.

concepts.partName: Triple Alliance and the Third Mysore War (1790–92)
concepts.bodyMd:
British power grew steadily in the Deccan, worrying Mysore ruler **Hyder Ali** on two fronts — the British and the Marathas. Hyder Ali defeated the British in the **First Mysore War (1766–68)** and fought them again in the **Second Mysore War (1780–84)**, dying in 1782. His son **Tipu Sultan** concluded the Mangalore treaty with the British in 1784, though the British felt badly humiliated in both wars.

The British sought Nizam Ali's help to defeat Tipu; the Marathas also agreed to join. The British, Nizam, and Marathas formed the **Triple Alliance** in July 1790 and declared war on Mysore — the **Third Mysore War (1790–92)**. Tipu tried, unsuccessfully, to win over the Nizam and Marathas. Finding Tipu difficult to defeat, General Medos judged direct intervention necessary, and Cornwallis personally surrounded Srirangapatnam. 

Tipu lost and agreed to the **Treaty of Srirangapatnam**, ceding half his state to the three allied parties. Nizam Ali received Gurramkonda, Kadapa, Gandikota, Khammam, and Ballery as his share. The British showed resentment toward the Nizam, feeling Prince Sikandarjah and Minister Azeem-ul-Umra had driven the Nizam's forces slowly through the war.

concepts.partName: The Loss of Kharda (1795)
concepts.bodyMd:
After the Third Mysore War, disputes resumed between the Marathas and the Nizam. Nizam Ali resisted Maratha collection of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi in his territory; in 1791, **Nana Fadnavis**, the Peshwa's minister, demanded these dues. Nizam Ali had long tried to weaken Maratha power by different methods, and now encouraged **Mahadaji Sindhia** against Fadnavis; the two agreed to work together, but Sindhia disclosed Nizam Ali's plan to Fadnavis, who ordered immediate payment of the dues. Sindhia died on 12 February 1794, but Fadnavis stood firm.

On **11 March 1795** the two states fought the **Kharda War**. Nizam Ali requested British help, but British officer Captain Kirkpatrick rejected the request. The Nizam fought bravely but lost, and on 15 March 1795 agreed to an insulting treaty: Doulatabad, Ahmednagar, and Sholapur forts, together worth Rs. 34,50,000 in annual revenue, were handed to the Marathas, and the Nizam paid three crore rupees as war indemnity.

concepts.partName: Raymond Services
concepts.bodyMd:
Under an earlier pact of 1768, the British were obliged to help the Nizam whenever necessary, but they had not done so during the Kharda war. Afterward, Nizam Ali sent the British forces stationed in his territory back to British territory. He summoned Resident Captain Kirkpatrick to express his displeasure, stating that maintaining the two regular British battalions at heavy cost for so many years, without their actually being available for use, was meaningless, and had them removed from Hyderabad immediately.

Turning his attention instead to the French, Nizam Ali found their officer **Raymond** eager to please him. Raymond's French forces had fought at Kharda for the Nizam and lost 3,000 soldiers. Nizam Ali increased the "Raymond French Forces" to 15,000, paying a subsidy of Rs. 1,30,000 per month for their upkeep. Raymond asked for Kadapa to help maintain his forces and requested to be sent there under the pretext of providing security; **Mir Alam** informed Resident Kirkpatrick of these developments in 1795, heightening British anxiety over Nizam's activities.

At the same time, Nizam Ali's eldest son and Prince **Ali Jah** revolted against his father, reaching Bidar with the support of Medak Zamindar Sadashiva Reddy. Nizam Ali sought British help to suppress the revolt; British forces under Major Robert were sent toward Bidar. 

Ali Jah, seeing the situation, surrendered, and after a few days, on his way back to Hyderabad, he committed suicide on **22 November 1795**. Raymond's forces also assisted in suppressing this revolt. Raymond himself died on **25 March 1798**; after him, **Perron** took charge of the French forces, whose strength and influence subsequently declined.

concepts.partName: The Subsidiary Alliance (1798)
concepts.bodyMd:
**Lord Wellesley** was appointed Governor-General on 17 May 1798, succeeding Sir John Shore. British officials judged that Nizam's support was essential both to control Tipu Sultan and the Marathas, and to remove French influence from the Deccan. 

Wellesley ordered Kirkpatrick to conclude a new security treaty with the Nizam; Kirkpatrick explained its terms and Nizam Ali signed it on **1 September 1798** — known as the **Subsidiary Alliance**. Where two British battalions had previously served the Nizam, six more were added to protect the state, for which the Nizam was required to pay **Rs. 24,17,100 every year** to maintain the six battalions. Hyderabad thereby became a protected state of the British.

concepts.partName: Fourth Mysore War & The Ceded Districts (1799–1800)
concepts.bodyMd:
### Fourth Mysore War (1799)

Wellesley, as Governor-General, moved to control Tipu Sultan and declared war against Mysore in 1799 — the **Fourth Mysore War**. Nizam Ali supported the British; Mir Alam led Nizam forces, which met British forces under General Harris at Nellore, and together they marched on Srirangapatnam. 

Tipu fought to the last and died defending his state; the combined British and Nizam forces won. By the resulting treaty, the British handed over Gooty, Gurramkonda, and Jerimulla in Chitradurg and Kolar regions to the Nizam, while the remaining, smaller Mysore territory was restored to the royal Wadayar family. The Nizam was dissatisfied that the British had kept the strategically valuable regions while he received the ordinary ones.

### The Ceded Districts (1800)

After Tipu Sultan's death, Wellesley remained concerned about the continued strength of the Marathas in the Deccan and sought a stronger alliance with the Nizam to counter them. A fresh treaty was concluded on **20 October 1800**, under which the Subsidiary Alliance forces were further increased — one more Cavalry regiment along with proportional guns, artillery men, and eight battalions for the Nizam State. 

In exchange, the territories the Nizam had gained under the Srirangapatnam treaty (18 March 1792) and the Mysore treaty (22 June 1799) were permanently ceded to the British for maintaining these forces in Hyderabad: **Bellary, Anantapur, Kadapa, and Kurnool districts** — thereafter known as the **Ceded Districts**. This 1800 treaty reduced the Nizam to the position of a subservient ally of the British. 

A commercial treaty followed in 1802, under which goods produced in either state paid a 5 percent tax when entering the other; Hyderabad also collected a 5 percent tax on British imports. Nizam Ali died in 1803, shortly after this treaty.

concepts.partName: Sikandar Jah (1803–1829)
concepts.bodyMd:
**Sikandar Jah**, Nizam Ali's second son, ruled from 1803 to 1829 (Ali Jah, the elder son, had already revolted and died by suicide in 1795). Secunderabad city was named after him.

### Second Maratha War and Territorial Gains

War between the Marathas and the British began in 1803, soon after Sikandar Jah's accession — the **Second Maratha War**. Under the 1800 treaty, the Nizam was obliged to send all his forces, but he chose not to; only a small contingent went, under the control of his friend, Berar Governor Mahipat Ram, with Salabat Khan (Nawab of Ellichpur) and Raja Shukradar responsible for escorting them to the front — though in action the Nizam forces did not actively help the British.

On **23 September 1803**, at Assai, the British defeated the Marathas. The Nizam received Maratha territory as his share of the victory: the Ajantha hills, the middle Godavari region, land south of the Satpura mountains, and Nagpur-king-held districts west of the Wardha river — bringing the entire Berar region under Nizam control and extending the Nizam's territory considerably. 

Wellesley wrote to the Nizam expressing resentment against certain nobles and the general of the Nizam's army during the war; the Nizam compromised and concluded a treaty on 15 December 1803, adding a further article on 9 January 1804 providing for mutual co-operation between civil and military officers and open access to forts and regions during wartime. 

**Azim-ul-Umra**, Diwan (Prime Minister) of Hyderabad, died on 12 April 1804, shortly after the treaty; **Mir Alam**, favourable to the British, was appointed Diwan in his place.

### Chandulal and the Rise of British Influence

The Nizam wanted his friend Mahipat Ram as Diwan instead of Mir Alam, but the British preferred Mir Alam, who was accordingly appointed. When the post of Peshkar fell vacant, the Nizam wished to appoint Mahipat Ram, but Mir Alam's son-in-law Munir-ul-Mulk and Raja Chandulal contested it; the Nizam sent Mahipat Ram to Berar, and **Chandulal** was appointed Peshkar, though the Nizam had no good opinion of him — his appointment came through British pressure and Mir Alam's influence. 

Chandulal continued as Peshkar with the support of British Resident **Syden Ham**. Mir Alam died on 28 February 1808, and the post of Diwan fell vacant; Munir-ul-Mulk and Shams-ul-Umra contested it. The British Governor-General proposed Shams-ul-Umra, but the Nizam disagreed, and Munir-ul-Mulk was finally appointed Diwan, while Chandulal continued as Peshkar.

In 1810 Syden Ham was transferred from Hyderabad, and **Russell** came as the new Resident, taking over administration and powers through Chandulal — the Resident thereby playing a key role in Hyderabad state administration. From 1811 onwards, Nizam Sikandar Jah took no interest in administration.

### The Russell Brigade

Russell arrived as Resident in 1811 and immediately reported the atrocities of Zamindars in Hyderabad to the British Bengal Government. He noted that the Nizam's forces were not being used for internal crises, and found three types of Nizam forces poorly managed: the Nizam's own private army (neglected since the 1800 treaty), a Diwan-controlled force made up largely of Rohillas (also acting irresponsibly), and a third force, the Linewala, formed by Mahipat Ram and based in Berar. Since all three acted irresponsibly, Russell sought to reorganize the Nizam's forces.

With the permission of the Indian Government, Russell established a separate force called the **'Russell Brigade'**, later evolved into the **'Hyderabad Contingent.'** It took part in the Maratha war of 1818, suppressed the Pindaris in 1817, and controlled local revolts from 1818–1820. 

Russell captured **Mubariz-ul-Doula** and **Shams-ud-Doula**, who were opposing the British, and with Nizam Sikander Jah's help sent them as prisoners — first to the Nizam's palace on 23 August 1815, then to Golconda fort, where they were imprisoned until their release in 1820.

The Nizam became permanently free from the Marathas after the Marathas lost the **Third Maratha War (1818)**; Vizapur, the Kannada talukas, and the Ellora and Aurangabad talukas were merged into Hyderabad state, and the Nizam was freed from Chauth and Sardeshmukhi levies. 

However, the expenditure of the Russell Brigade proved unbearable; Russell, judging it impossible for the Nizam to pay these costs directly, arranged for the state to take loans from the **Palmer and Palmer Company** to fund the forces' salaries.

### Palmer and Palmer Company

Palmer and Palmer Company was a business house founded by **William Palmer**, who had started his career in Nizam service in 1791 as the first British citizen to join the Nizam army, rising to the rank of Brigadier before retiring in 1812 to start a business career. He applied to the Governor-General's Council on 30 March 1814 for permission to open a bank in Hyderabad and received it; Russell took a keen interest in the bank's establishment. 

Members of the company included William Palmer, Hastings Palmer, William Karri (Resident Surgeon), Bankati Das, Shamul Russell, South Be, George Lamb, and Engineer Russell.

**Economic exploitation**: The company took deposits from individuals at 12 percent interest and lent money at 25 percent interest. Chandulal obtained British Government permission in 1819 for a loan of 60,00,000 rupees; the Palmer Company agreed to disburse this in six installments at 18 percent interest, while itself receiving 24,00,000 per year from the Nizam Government and taking the Berar district (worth Rs. 30,00,000 revenue) on lease from the Nizam — a transaction yielding the company a profit of Rs. 6,00,000. 

Palmer family members additionally drew pensions of Rs. 30,000 each per month from the Hyderabad treasury. This affair gave rise to the popular sayings **"Nizam Looted"** and **"All Pay Nizzy"** current in the Deccan at the time. William Rambold, son-in-law of the Madras Governor and relative of Governor-General Hastings, joined as a shareholder in 1816, after which the exploitation reached its peak; it continued until 1820, when **Metcalf** arrived as Resident and brought it under control.

### Reforms of Metcalf

**Charles Metcalf** was appointed Resident of Hyderabad in place of Henry Russell in December 1820. He quickly recognized how the Palmer and Palmer Company was exploiting the state, provided the Nizam with a loan facility from the Government of India at 6 percent interest, and freed the Nizam from the Palmer Company, which went bankrupt within a year. 

The Nizam took Rs. 7,00,000 from the British Government to clear the Palmer Company dues, and permanently handed over his rights on the Northern Circar peshkash to the British on 4 November 1823.

Metcalf carried through administrative reforms in Hyderabad:

*   Ordered revenue collection on Khalsa, Jagir, and Jatidad lands based on net production.
*   Reviewed expenditure on forces and pensions, identifying a Rs. 10,00,000 deficit in Nizam Government revenue.
*   Fixed village-level peasant tax payments to the government, calculated land value village by village, and reported this to the government.
*   Appointed European officers to receive peasant complaints directly, giving peasants a channel to reach the Nizam.
*   Gave European supervisors powers to check crimes and atrocities committed by feudal lords.
*   Appointed hereditary police officers.
*   Concluded a new treaty with the Nizam in 1822, exempting the Nizam from the Chouth levy.

These reforms systematized the Hyderabad state. Metcalf left Hyderabad in 1825. Nizam Sikandar Jah died on **21 May 1829**.

concepts.partName: Nasir-ud-Doula (1829–1857)
concepts.bodyMd:
The Government of India recognized Sikandar Jah's son, **Nasir-ud-Doula**, as the next Nizam. On acceding, he removed the European superintendents appointed under the Metcalf reforms. Hyderabad forces under Minister Chandulal controlled revolts by the Zamindars of Mungal, Amalapalem, Mensur, Chitagani, and Hingoli, and by the Zamindars of Bheed (Dharmaji Appa Rao), Hatkar, Nowa (Nousoji Naik), Veerappa Naik of Koppal, Venkata Narsinga Rao of Amalapalem, and the Zamindars of Chintagani, Munagala, Sironcha, and Mahadevapuram — all revolting against European attacks or official domination. 

Hyderabad forces gradually controlled these revolts. **General Fraser** was appointed Resident in 1838; around this time, the Wahabi movement reached the Deccan.

### The Wahabi Movement

**Syed Ahmed Brailvey** started the Wahabi Movement in India, active first in Bengal, the North-Western frontiers, and the United Provinces during the 1820s, aimed against Sikh dominance in Punjab. Syed Ahmad's followers, called **Muzahids**, were urged by him in a letter to Sikandar Jah to be given wealth and forces to fight not only the Sikhs but also the Europeans and their domination.

Syed Ahmad himself died in 1831; his followers reached the Deccan in 1838, led by **Moulvi Vilayat Ali and Saleem**, who came to trust **Mubariz-ud-Doula** and made him their leader in India.

Mubariz-ud-Doula started a revolt against the British. Captain Malcom informed Resident General Fraser of the revolt and of Mubariz's secret contact with rulers of different regions; Fraser discussed the matter with the Nizam for his arrest, and Nizam Nasir-ud-Doula finally sent his own brother to Golconda fort. 

The Tonku, Rampur, Udayagiri, and Kurnool Nawabs supported the Wahabi Movement and joined it against the British, but the British suppressed and controlled them. Mubariz-ud-Doula died on **25 June 1854** in Golconda fort under government custody; the Wahabi Movement declined after his death.

### The Cession of Berar (1853)

By January 1851, the Nizam's dues to the British East India Company had reached Rs. 70,00,000. The Nizam had promised to pay Rs. 12,00,000 annually to clear the dues, but Governor-General **Lord Dalhousie** was strict and wrote demanding immediate full payment. **Siraj-ul-Mulk** was appointed Diwan on 29 June 1851; he paid half the due amount, Rs. 34,08,485, on 15 August 1851 to build British confidence, promising the balance by 31 October 1851 — but only Rs. 8,73,547 more was paid by year's end. **Colonel John Low** was appointed the new Resident of Hyderabad in 1853.

Low held that a definite arrangement was needed from the Nizam's Government for controlled monthly expenditure by the British and pressed the Nizam to hand over district revenues directly to the British. With no option left, the Nizam signed the **Berar Treaty on 21 May 1853**, under which Berar state, Osmanabad, and Raichur districts were handed to the British. Diwan Siraj-ul-Mulk died shortly after, on 23 May 1853; his son-in-law **Salarjung** was appointed the new Diwan.

### Summary

The British used the Hyderabad state to serve their economic needs and those of their forces, acquiring fertile lands and mineral-rich regions from the state between 1766 and 1853 through a succession of treaties. They grew economically strong through control of the Northern Circars, the Ceded Districts, and Berar. 

The Nizam opposed British policy at several points, but with little effect given his relative weakness against British power; figures such as Mir Alam and Chandulal, along with other government officials, aided the British in this process, alongside British political manoeuvring, which contributed to the Nizams' declining standing. 

Hyderabad faced repeated difficulties arising from Russell's and John Low's policies, and the Nizam had to struggle each time war broke out with the Marathas or the Mysore state. From 1853 onward, the Nizam's Hyderabad state moved toward modernity.
